title: Run Frontier AI at Home — Alex Cheema, EXO Labs
talk_summary: Alex Cheema of EXO Labs describes running frontier open models locally by co-designing across the stack: fusing inefficient kernels, splitting prefill (compute-bound) from decode (memory-bound) across heterogeneous devices, and clustering Macs/GPUs with low-latency RDMA. The talk is mostly about local inference hardware economics, with a few transferable points about harness quality, batching via multi-agent/test-time compute, and skepticism toward auto-research without the scientific method.

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues the harness matters as much as the model: a good harness keeps the prompt prefix (system prompt, tools) stable so prefill gets cache hits, and notes the same model performs differently under different harnesses.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you use closed code with a certain model, and then use open code with exactly the same model, you get completely different performance

takeaways.technique: Batch via parallel agents / best-of-N instead of batch size 1
takeaways.what_they_do: Notes that a single user request in an agentic system is already multiple concurrent model calls, so local/self-hosted inference gets effective batch >1; similarly best-of-N test-time search creates parallelism.

takeaways.technique: Open benchmark matrix over configs, not cherry-picked single runs
takeaways.what_they_do: Continuously benchmark many models/quantizations/pruning configs and publish a Pareto frontier of quality vs speed vs cost so buyers can pick by budget instead of trusting noisy anecdotes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we want to publish benchmarks in the open that show you, okay, what performance will I get on certain hardware

takeaways.what_they_do: Warns that auto-research loops without a hypothesis and controlled experiment produce cherry-picked, unusable results, and that LLMs will tell you you made a breakthrough when you didn't.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if it's just like, 'Oh, hey, auto research, go off and figure out how to make this fast.' It won't work

takeaways.technique: Split compute-bound prefill from memory-bound decode across hosts
takeaways.what_they_do: Runs prefill on a high-compute GPU and streams the KV cache to a high-memory-bandwidth device for decode, overlapping communication with compute; got ~2x end-to-end on large prompts.
takeaways.numbers: ~2x faster end-to-end on ~100KB prompts; RDMA cut inter-node latency from ~300µs to single-digit µs

takeaways.technique: Diminishing returns: match model size to task, not max intelligence
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues most use cases follow an S-curve where beyond a threshold more intelligence yields little utility, so smaller/cheaper models suffice for routine tasks while frontier models are reserved for hard problems.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's not kind of just unlimited returns on intelligence... there's a certain point where you just don't need any more intelligence to do something
